metadata.title: My Tiny Garo Villages Christmas Celebrations
metadata.description:
Christmas celebrations among us the Garos or A’chiks as we call ourselves, of the Meghalaya is a grand community affair and I make sure that, I show up for Christmas celebrations at my village no matter where I am based out of. That is the time when not just I but almost everyone who stays, works or studies far from home, shows up at their ancestral village. Around the Christmas time it looks as if the hundreds of tiny obscure villages scattered all across the difficult mountainous terrains of Meghalaya are having some sort of annual grand re-union. 

Apart from the harvest festival ‘Wangala’, Christmas is the most important festival for us Garos, as most of the Garo population follows Christianity. The preparation for the celebration usually starts weeks before the actual day of Christmas itself. People who have come from different places visit homes of friends and relative and catch up with each other over enormous servings of piping hot black tea and Garo rice cakes known as Sakin. 

People sitting outdoors around a fire with unending supply of tea pouring in, is a common sight during the festive season. Sometimes people sit around the fire soaking up the warmth and enjoy each other’s company without even exchange of words. 

About a week ahead of the Christmas Men folks of the village hold a meeting and decide to erect a huge bamboo pandal in the centre of the village, By huge I mean enormous, the pandal can house the entire village population.  The young and even the old folks of the village work together in erecting the pandal, people collect mature bamboo poles from the forest, others collect paddy straw from the fields for the flooring. Rules a bit stringent, if one fails to socialize and does not participate in the setting up process for the pandal, they are fined a sum of Rs. 250/-. Only the really young and the really old are exempted from this. 

Each household is tasked with bringing in their quota of fire-wood for cooking the Christmas feast and for burning to keep the pandal warm throughout the night.  The village elders decide, select and buy Pigs and chickens a day in advance of the feast for slaughtering. 

We are generally frugal eaters, our food is usually is serving of steamed rice with boiled vegetable and few pieces of meat. It has no glamour quotient in food that you can see in the mainland India. However, we don’t mind loosening our purse strings when it comes to festivals and we go way overboard during the Christmas celebrations.

Our cooking is no different from the rest of North-east; we prefer pork over other meat, the Christmas feast is incomplete sans the pork. The menu that’s served during the Christmas feast has remained unchanged since my childhood, at least in my village.  Usually for the feast, Pork and Chicken stew thickened with pounded rice, known as Pura is served with a side of hot and spicy pork and chicken fry. The dish is served wrapped in leaves of a plant locally known as Reru (Pyrnium Pubinerve).
Steamed rice is your liability and you need to bring the rice along with you for the feast. People also bring their own home-cooked sumptuous sides. The feast actually doubles up as a huge pot-luck dinner too. People after a brief prayer, sit together in the pandal and have the dinner together sharing each other’s sides. 

Following the feast, various traditional cultural programs are organised, which is incomplete without the men vs women riddle battle, where the opposite gender take on each other with witty jibes. Trust me it’s bloodbath out there.

After all the programs are over, the old, the young and even the really really old, who can barely walk normal circumstances, I mean the toothless, hunchbacked old ones dance the night away to songs and drum beats. The drum beats coming from distant villages scattered all across the jungles resonates throughout the night until the morning, true to the words of the Garo song that we usually dance to “salgi a’aa mo’o ba dontongkuna be” which translates as “Even if the sky and shakes do not stop dancing and celebrating.”

The Garos of the North-eastern India are no different from any other North-eastern tribes in India; we are fun loving, simple hearted and hard working people.
